bib.title: Effective Long-Context Scaling of Foundation Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Effective Long-Context Scaling of Foundation Models. Wenhan Xiong, Jingyu Liu (equal contribution), Igor Molybog, Hejia Zhang, et al., up to Mike Lewis, Sinong Wang, Hao Ma. GenAI, Meta. arXiv:2309.16039v3 [cs.CL], 14 Nov 2023. Preprint (no venue printed).
COVERAGE: Read all 23 pages (73,466 chars). I skimmed the reference list. I read the appendices, including A (more results), B (theory, only partly), C (extrapolation) and D (self-instruct prompts). The Appendix B math was read only in outline. Figure 9 and Figure 7 are image-only and were not read.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- The 70B model's validation loss follows a power law with context length up to 32,768 tokens, with diminishing returns. Larger models have a larger beta, so they use context better.
  number: L(c) = (alpha/c)^beta + gamma. Fitted values by model size: 7B alpha=25.4, beta=0.45, gamma=1.56; 13B 19.5/0.48/1.45; 34B 17.7/0.50/1.41; 70B 17.9/0.51/1.35. Doubling the context multiplies the reducible loss by 2^-beta, about 0.7 for 70B.
  setup: Llama 2 Long models, validation language-modeling loss, context up to 32k. The 70B model was trained at 16k sequences and the 7B/13B at 32k. This is a loss result, not a task result.
  quote: "if we double the context length, we can expect the loss to be reduced by a factor of 2−β ≈ 0.7 plus a model specific constant (1 − 2−β) · γ." Also: "Larger models can leverage the contexts more effectively, indicated by the largerβ value of the curves."
  where: p.5 (Sec 3.1); Fig 1 on p.1

- Task scores improve monotonically as the maximum input length grows from 4k to 16k (70B).
  number: NarrativeQA F1 27.5, 28.7, 30.2, 30.9; Qasper F1 28.9, 32.7, 35.1, 35.7; QuALITY EM 63.9, 80.3, 79.6, 79.7; QMSum ROUGE-geo 10.9, 11.9, 14.4, 16.5, at max input 4,096, 8,192, 12,288 and 16,384 respectively.
  setup: Llama 2 Long 70B, pretrained model, left-truncated prompts. The values are read from the Fig 2 extraction.
  quote: "we first show in Figure 2 that the results on each long task improve monotonically as we increase the context lengths."
  Caution: the QuALITY numbers in the extraction (63.9, 80.3, 79.6, 79.7) are flat after 8k and not strictly monotonic. Only the text claims monotonic.
  where: p.5, Fig 2

- Llama 2's RoPE could not attend usefully beyond about 4,000-6,000 tokens, even after long continual pretraining. Raising the RoPE base frequency from 10,000 to 500,000 (RoPE ABF) fixed this.
  number: 4,000-6,000 tokens effective window before; base frequency 10,000 to 500,000.
  setup: 7B model, synthetic FIRST-SENTENCE-RETRIEVAL probe (the model returns the first sentence of the input). Variants were continually pretrained with 80B tokens on 32,768-token sequences.
  quote: "our model was unable to effectively attend beyond 4, 000 - 6, 000 tokens even after extensive long-context continual pretraining." and "increasing the “base frequency b” of ROPE from 10, 000 to 500, 000". Also: "ROPE ABF is the only variant that can maintain its performance up to the full 32,768-token context window on theFIRST-SENTENCE -RETRIEVAL task."
  where: p.7-8 (Sec 4.1)

- The effective context window can be much shorter than the nominal window, and it needs a probe task to find it. The authors say perplexity and synthetic tasks alone are not enough.
  number: none
  setup: The authors criticise earlier long-context work that measured only loss and synthetic tasks. They add real tasks (NarrativeQA, Qasper, QuALITY, QMSum, ZeroSCROLLS, L-Eval).
  quote: "which do not comprehensively demonstrate their effectiveness in diverse, real-world scenarios." Also, on Passkey: "We believe this task is overly simple for context probing." Of the PE variants, "All the model variants except ROPE can achieve perfect accuracy."
  where: p.2, p.8 footnote 4

- Long-context continual pretraining reached nearly the same quality as pretraining on long sequences from scratch, with about 40% fewer FLOPs.
  number: FLOPs 3.783e22 (32k from scratch) vs 3.405e22, 3.026e22 and 2.270e22 for switching at 20%, 40% and 80%. At 40% switch NarrativeQA F1 20.1 vs 18.5 from scratch; Qasper 27.0 vs 28.6.
  setup: 7B model, 4k to 32k switch at 20%, 40% or 80% of training, same total tokens, 4M tokens per gradient update.
  quote: "continual pretraining from short context models can easily save around 40% FLOPs while imposing almost no loss on performance."
  where: p.10, Tables 10-11

- Long documents in the pretraining data matter less than data quality.
  number: Relative gain over Llama 2 7B: QuALITY +75.5% (Llama 2 Long mix) vs +67.1% (long text removed) vs +65.0% (long text upsampled). QMSum +45.70% vs +36.60% vs +42.83%. NarrativeQA +23.70% vs +19.48% vs +22.15%.
  setup: 7B continual pretraining, prompts truncated at 16,384 tokens, relative improvement over the 4,096-token Llama 2 7B.
  quote: "even with most of the long texts removed, the model can still obtain most of the performance gain over LLAMA 2." and "the improvements of our pretrain data over the one used by LLAMA 2 mostly come from the quality of the data itself, instead of the length distribution difference."
  where: p.9, Table 7

- The 70B chat model beats gpt-3.5-turbo-16k on 7 of 10 ZeroSCROLLS tasks, with no human-annotated long data.
  number: Average 37.7 vs 36.7 (gpt-3.5-turbo-16k), 34.0 (gpt-3.5-turbo 4k), 39.1 (Claude 8k), 41.7 (GPT-4 8k). Individual tasks: QuALITY 82.6 vs 72.0; QMSum 20.0 vs 17.4; NarrativeQA 31.7 vs 29.5. It trails GPT-4 and Claude on average.
  setup: Llama 2 Long Chat 70B, ZeroSCROLLS benchmark configuration. gpt-3.5-turbo-16k was evaluated 8/7/2023. The GPT-4 and Claude numbers were copied from the leaderboard.
  quote: "our 70B chat model is able to outperform gpt-3.5-turbo-16k on 7 out of the 10 tasks."
  where: p.6, Table 4

- Instruction tuning: adding language-modeling loss on the long input prompt helps the self-instruct data. Short-only RLHF data already gives a decent long model.
  number: Qasper 35.7 to 38.9; QuALITY 59.3 to 77.3; QMSum 13.4 to 18.5 (self-inst w/o LM loss vs with). Llama 2 Chat baseline: Qasper 12.2, QuALITY 56.7.
  setup: Table 9, Llama 2 Long fine-tuned with different data mixes.
  quote: "we find it particularly beneficial to also calculate the language modeling loss on the long input prompts"
  where: p.3, p.10, Table 9

- Long-context training did not hurt short tasks, and mostly improved them.
  number: Llama 2 70B vs Llama 2 Long 70B: MMLU 68.9 vs 71.7; Math 35.2 vs 41.3; Coding 37.4 vs 39.9; GSM8K 56.8 vs 65.4 (Table 2). The 7B comparison is Coding 16.8 vs 20.6, MMLU 45.3 vs 47.8.
  setup: Table 1 aggregates. The authors attribute this to extra FLOPs and the newly introduced long data.
  quote: "we observe on-par and, in most cases, stronger results than LLAMA 2."
  where: p.4

- Extending the window cost little compute per step, and attention was not the bottleneck at these lengths.
  number: About 17% speed loss going from 4,096 to 16,384 tokens (70B). Attention cost dominates only past 49,152 (6h) tokens, with h=8192.
  setup: Llama 2 70B, FlashAttention, same tokens per batch.
  quote: "we observe around 17% speed loss when increasing the sequence length from 4,096 to 16,384 for the 70B model."
  where: p.3

- Extrapolation beyond the training length is weak. The Llama 2 4k baseline's loss explodes past its training length. For Llama 2 Long 70B, loss holds in the extrapolation area, but FIRST-SENTENCE-RETRIEVAL degrades when extrapolating.
  number: none (shown in a figure only)
  setup: 70B trained at 16,384, tested to 32,768.
  quote: "the loss explodes after the position goes beyond training sequence length" and "we do see some performance degradation when the model needs to extrapolate."
  where: App. C, p.22 (Fig 9)

- Long inputs have a token cost that depends on the tokenizer. This is the budgeting point.
  number: about 10% more tokens than GPT-3.5's tokenizer
  setup: Llama tokenizer, 32k vocabulary
  quote: "we observe our tokenizer often produce 10% more tokens on average."
  where: p.13 (Sec 6)

- Input truncation is a confound in long-context benchmarks. Left truncation was used.
  number: 16,384-token cap; 32,768 also tested (Table 13, e.g. Llama 2 Long 13B QuALITY 57.6 at 16k vs 59.0 at 32k)
  quote: "The input prompts are truncated from the left side if the prompts exceed the maximum input length of the model or 16,384 tokens." and "truncating the input context might also remove the information necessary to answer the question."
  where: p.4, p.6

- Human evaluation covered 2,352 examples across multi-turn chat and multi-document search QA. The model was competitive with MPT-30B-chat, GPT-3.5-turbo-16k and Claude-2.
  number: 2,352 examples, 3 annotators each, 95% CI. The win-rate values are only in Fig 3, which is an image.
  quote: "We focus on two major application scenarios with a total of 2,352 examples."
  where: p.7

LIMITS
- The authors concede that automatic metrics are limited and that leakage into proprietary models cannot be ruled out.
- The model is not tuned for long-form outputs such as creative writing.
- Hallucination is a problem, and it is "more pronounced" for long-context models.
- Safety: a long-context safety benchmark does not exist. The red teaming was internal and manual.
- Long-context prompt injection risk is noted via Greshake et al., 2023.
- Evidence is from Llama 2 only, with 7B/13B trained at 32k and 34B/70B at 16k. There is no study of mid-context position bias ("lost in the middle") and no needle-in-a-haystack test. The retrieval probe is first-sentence only.
- Results are from 2023 and cover open models. Proprietary comparisons (GPT-4 8k, Claude 8k, gpt-3.5-turbo-16k) have dated.
- The Llama 2 4k to 32k extension is now old, and newer models have much longer windows.
- Everything here is about the model, not about how to budget a prompt. The note's budgeting claims will need the paper's numbers framed as capability evidence.

BUILDS ON
- Llama 2 (Touvron et al., 2023)
- RoPE (Su et al., 2022)
- Position Interpolation (Chen et al., 2023)
- Code Llama (Rozière et al., 2023), which concurrently proposed the base-frequency idea
- XPos (Sun et al., 2022)
- FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022)
- Scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022)
- Self-Instruct (Wang et al., 2022)
- Passkey task (Mohtashami and Jaggi, 2023)
- ZeroSCROLLS (Shaham et al., 2023)
- L-Eval (An et al., 2023)
- Narayanan et al., 2021, for the attention-cost threshold
- Sparse attention (Child et al., 2019), which the authors chose not to use

CODE
Prompts in Appendix D (p.22-23) for generating long-context QA data. Verbatim, short form: "[INST] You are given a long text (delimited by triple quotes) and a question. Read the text and answer the question in the end. \"\"\"{FULL_DOCUMENT}\"\"\" Question: {QUESTION} [/INST] {ANSWER}". Evaluation prompt (footnote 2, p.4): "{CONTEXT } Q: {QUESTION }, A:".

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.1): validation loss versus context length with the power-law fits for each model size. Shows the scaling claim at a glance.
- Fig 2 (p.5): the four long tasks versus maximum input length 4k to 16k. This is the most useful figure for a budgeting note.
- Fig 4 (p.8): attention-score decay with distance under each PE variant. It shows why the base-frequency change was needed.
- Fig 5b (p.9): FIRST-SENTENCE-RETRIEVAL accuracy versus task length from 256 to 30k. It shows the effective window per PE variant.
- Fig 3 (p.6): human win rates, 95% CI. The values are not in the extracted text.

PROBLEMS: Figure values are not extractable except where numbers are printed as text (Fig 1, Fig 2). Greek letters were dropped in the Fig 1 legend, but the values are reconstructed from the Llama 2 Long legend order. I recommend checking the plot labels against alpha, beta, gamma in the original. Some table spacing was garbled, for example "QMSumF1". There were no embedded instructions in the PDF. Table 4 was extracted as a flat row, so per-column mapping to task names was inferred from the header. The 70B 3-task numbers are mapped by column order (GR, SS, QM, SQAL, Qspr, Nrtv, QALT, MuSQ, SpDg, BkSS), so check them against the PDF before citing.
